Year after curbs on content takedown powers, Centre weighs allowing junior cops to probe cybercrime

Section 78 of IT Act bars officers below Inspector rank from investigating offences under the law. Centre's high-level committee on digital arrest scams has backed amending the law.

Vrinda Tulsian

New Delhi: The central government’s high-level committee on digital arrest scams has backed amending the Information Technology Act to let police officers below the rank of Inspector investigate specified cybercrime offences. The minutes, however, do not specify which offences would be covered.

The proposal has been recorded in the minutes of the inter-departmental committee’s 24 September meeting, chaired by the Special Secretary (Internal Security) in the Union Home Ministry. The minutes are annexed to the ministry’s fifth status report to the Supreme Court—seen by ThePrint—filed on 7 October in a suo motu case on digital arrest scams.

Section 78 of the IT Act bars any officer below Inspector rank from investigating offences under the law.

Show Full Article

This proposal comes a year after the IT ministry—in October 2025—amended the IT Rules, so that only police officers of Deputy Inspector General rank or above could issue content takedown notices to platforms.

The 24 September minutes state that the “limited availability of officers of the required rank, particularly Inspectors in specialised cybercrime units, may create an operational bottleneck if the number of FIRs increases substantially”. The committee “considered the need of the suitable amendment”, under which officers “below the present prescribed rank may be empowered to investigate specified cybercrime offences”.

The committee has sought data from I4C, the Union home ministry and the Union IT ministry, so that it can examine “the feasibility of empowering suitably trained officers of lower rank, subject to appropriate safeguards and qualifications”. I4C is an initiative of the Ministry of Home Affairs linked to cybercrime that became an attached office of the ministry in July 2024.

Also Read: Meta tells govt it acted on 61k ‘inciteful posts’ in 2 weeks; claims 95% drop in AI content on platforms

Why the change The trigger behind the proposal is the e-Zero FIR system, which automatically converts large cybercrime complaints into FIRs. According to the minutes of the panel’s meeting, it has raised the share of complaints registered as FIRs from one-two percent to about eight percent.

The offences covered under IT Act range from hacking and identity theft, to publishing or transmitting “obscene” material online under Section 67, a provision police have also invoked over social media posts. Parliament last changed the rank requirement in 2008, lowering it from Deputy Superintendent of Police to Inspector. Several High Courts have, over time , held that IT Act investigations by officers below Inspector rank do not meet the law’s requirement.

Immigration data & bank checks The status report details several other measures being undertaken.

The Central Bureau of Investigation’s report, annexed to the filing, says the agency met the Bureau of Immigration “for using the immigration travel database to curb misuse of international roaming connections operated from scam compounds abroad”. It adds that the “technical feasibility of sharing said information was discussed”. CBI presents the talks as a follow-up to its national cyber-crime conference in February this year.

At a 22 July meeting with the Department of Financial Services, and banks’ chief vigilance and technology officers, CBI secured agreement on several steps.

Every bank account is to be linked to the holder’s Aadhaar-verified mobile number. Biometric OTP checks are to be extended to the opening of accounts in all banks. Mule-account databases are to be shared among banks in real time, and the Reserve Bank of India’s AI tool, MuleHunter.AI, is to be strengthened “with IP logs and geolocation data”.

Telecom checks The Department of Telecommunications told the court in October that on 17 August, it directed telecom operators to block SIM cards issued beyond the legal limit.

Operators are to use a “table of mobile connections and images” made available to them on DoT’s Digital Intelligence Platform, and have until 30 November to comply. I4C also shares with DoT, every day, the mobile numbers reported by complainants on the national cybercrime portal. Operators are to deploy AI and machine-learning tools to “red flag suspect connections, to re-verify them in a time bound manner and to disconnect those which fail verification”.

The home ministry status report submitted in court also records a rise in grievances from account holders, whose bank accounts were frozen, or whose money was held during cybercrime investigations. They went from about 2,000 in May, to 93,041 by 30 September. In a May letter to state police chiefs, I4C said many grievances were being closed “with inadequate or unreasonable remarks”.

Another 983 petitions seeking to unfreeze accounts are pending in high courts. The petitioners include the stock-broking platform Groww, fintech firms such as RapiPay and Resilient Innovations—the company behind BharatPe—and small businesses and individuals.

The Supreme Court will hear the case next on 23 November.

(Edited by Mannat Chugh)

By Heekyong Yang SEOUL, Nov 14 (Reuters) – South Korea should neither fear China’s rise nor underestimate its capabilities, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on Saturday, urging deeper cooperation ahead of a regional summit in China next week.

“During this visit to China, I was reminded that we should neither have an unfounded fear of China’s rise nor underestimate its capabilities and potential,” Cho wrote on X, saying Seoul should build cooperation benefiting both countries by drawing on the autonomy and creativity of its people and companies.

Cho’s remarks came after talks and dinner with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Friday, their first meeting in about three months.

Show Full Article

The ministers discussed bilateral ties, issues on the Korean Peninsula and ways to deliver tangible benefits to people in both countries

The meeting came ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit in Shenzhen on November 18-19, which South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will attend. Lee is also scheduled to join a dinner hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Seoul has said.

The summit is expected to bring together several major world leaders. U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin next Thursday on the sidelines of APEC, with nuclear arms reductions among the issues on the agenda, the White House said.

Cho said Seoul would seek to use Lee’s visit to advance bilateral ties and expand “horizontal and mutually beneficial” cooperation in areas where the two countries have complementary strengths.

Lee’s administration has sought to improve relations with China, South Korea’s largest trading partner, after ties were strained under former president Yoon Suk Yeol, while maintaining Seoul’s security alliance with the United States.

Wang said on Friday that China wanted to expand cooperation with South Korea in traditional industries and emerging sectors including artificial intelligence and biomedicine. He said bilateral ties had returned to the right track after exchanges between the two countries’ leaders.

(Reporting by Heekyong YangEditing by Shri Navaratnam)

By Brad Brooks and Steve Gorman Nov 13 (Reuters) – A tanker ship collided with a luxury paddle wheeler docked in New Orleans on the Mississippi River on Friday, causing the cruise vessel to roll over and sink as passengers scurried to disembark and dozens were flung into the water.

All aboard the stricken ship were accounted for after harbor personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull fallen passengers to safety, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a press conference.

Hailing the outcome as “a miracle on the Mississippi,” she said 32 passengers from American Cruise Lines paddle wheeler American Heritage were hospitalized, but “none with any type of critical injuries.”

Show Full Article

Moreno said roughly 180 to 190 passengers and crew members were aboard the American Heritage at the time of the mishap. The cruise ship has a capacity for 150 passengers and was built in 2015, American Cruise Lines said on its website.

The accident occurred about midday when the tanker ship, the Atlantic Asphalt, “lost control and collided” with the docked cruise vessel, Moreno said.

As passengers began fleeing, the cruise ship started to sink and eventually “toppled over and flipped,” dumping people into the river, the mayor said.

Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said about 87 passengers from the American Heritage disembarked before the vessel capsized, according to the joint news site of the New Orleans Advocate and Times-Picayune.

Moreno credited a swift response by local, state and federal personnel and bystanders from other vessels for preventing any loss of life.

The US Coast Guard said in an emailed statement that all river traffic was closed in the vicinity of the accident following the collision.

Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham told the New Orleans Advocate that the tanker appeared to have experienced some sort of steering failure but the cause of the mishap remained under investigation.

American Cruise Lines said in an emailed statement that it was coordinating with the Coast Guard and local authorities.

“Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved,” the company said.

(Reporting by Brad Brooks and Steve Gorman; Additional reporting by Ismail Shakil, Christian Martinez and Ryan Jones; Editing by Edmund Klamann and William Mallard)

By David Shepardson, Doyinsola Oladipo and Rajesh Kumar Singh WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) – The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday after a communications failure at air traffic control centers caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest nationwide shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (0115 GMT), but warned that departures would resume gradually and it would take time for airlines to restore normal operations.

“It’s going to be slow,” Duffy told reporters at the White House.

Show Full Article

More than 6,600 flights were canceled and 8,600 delayed, with another 1,500 already canceled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline schedules for days.

Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports around the country.

The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

Duffy said the trouble began at 3:36 p.m., when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar and communications systems. Switches and routers carrying critical data became overloaded, producing inconsistent information and prompting the FAA to halt departures nationwide, he said.

“Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down,” Duffy said, adding at no stage did they completely lose radar or communications and were able to safely land thousands of planes.

Duffy said the immediate problem had been fixed and that flying was safe, but warned that a broader overhaul of the aging air traffic control system was needed to prevent similar failures.

$50 BILLION AVIATION OVERHAUL

Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for $50 billion to modernize it.

Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging airports and air traffic control infrastructure.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said.

“Give us the money to fix it.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “zero evidence” so far that the outage resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue AI system, though investigators had not ruled out either possibility.

“It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we’re still looking,” Mullin said.

The National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation, he added.

The only other nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for about 90 minutes.

Investors were already pricing in a financial hit to airlines. Shares of American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines fell between 1% and 2% in after-hours trading, while JetBlue Airways dropped about 3%.

(Reporting by David Shepardson, Jasper Ward, Dan Catchpole, Rajesh Kumar Singh, Kristina Cooke, Bhargav Acharya, Anshuman Tripathy and Chris Sanders; Writing by Joe Brock; Editing by Caitlin Webber, Franklin Paul and Rod Nickel; Editing by Stephen Coates)
